sources.citation: Gotxu Weyaxaji Bujoum [Waxe New Testament]. 2014. 'Waxe - GGT', (c) 2014 Global Partners (find.bible id WTKE360; YouVersion version 3412). With earlier portions: Mak, Efesus dotu Kolosi [Mark, Ephesians, Colossians in Watakataui], 1991 (find.bible id WTK1991).
sources.note: Primary text only (scripture translation); no linguistic front matter online. Orthography sample (Mark 1:1-2): 'Jon Maxafe Baftais Xukuxeya Jisasxu Yaxatux Afaidobéjaja / Ande bujoum bex omombéjime profét Aisaiyaxeya.. xéfénasakouku imax nénéxuwaxa féto onma xeyoxébaja onéxu yaxatux aifsibaja' — the acute-accented é recurs several times within one word, so it evidently marks a vowel quality, not stress. Its existence implies an unpublished orthography/phonology statement held by the translating mission (a 23-year programme, 1991-2014), not located online.

sources.citation: Sumbuk, Kenneth Memson. 1999. Morphosyntax of Sare. PhD thesis, University of Waikato. xiii+335 pp. (hdl 10289/13888). Ch.1 with Chart 1.1 'The position of Sare within the Sepik area Papuan languages (Laycock 1973)'; 2.2.1 Stress (pp.40-42) for Sare/Kapriman only.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Read held by the project: the thesis describes Sare (Kapriman, kapr1245) only; p.2 'Of the Sepik Hill Family, to which Sare belongs, only Alamblak (Bruce 1984), has a comprehensive description'; the explicit stress rule (2.2.1, pp.40-42: secondary stress initial, primary stress final in disyllables and penultimate in longer words) is for Sare alone; nothing on this language.

sources.citation: Yamada, Yoichi (山田陽一). 1989. ワヘイのうた・霊の語り: パプアニューギニアの一社会における音の民族誌 [Wahei no uta, rei no katari: an ethnography of sound in a Papua New Guinea society]. PhD dissertation (学術博士, 甲第04007号), Osaka University. 389 pp. hdl:11094/29160; doi:10.11501/11358971. [Listed on verification as print/record-only; open copy located, downloaded and read by B.]
sources.note: Ethnography of sound (weeping, spirit narration, song, bamboo flutes). Its language section 'ワヘイ語表記' (pp. 11-12) gives the practical orthography against phonemes: vowels i e a o u (length written ':'); plosives p b t d k g, q (voiceless uvular), j = /G/ (voiced uvular), gw kw (labialised); fricatives f, s (~ʃ), x (uvular /ʁ/~/χ/); nasals m n ny; trill r; lateral l; semivowels w y; /a/ and /o/ vary by speaker 'but not distinctively'; 'what needs special care in Waxei pronunciation is the three uvulars written q, j, x'. Note 7: grammar omitted except that nouns mark gender and number (masc. sg.…

sources.citation: Bruce, Leslie Peter. 1979. A grammar of Alamblak (Papua New Guinea). PhD thesis, Australian National University. 572 pp. (Ch. 'Alamblak and the Middle Sepik languages', pp. 472-531).
sources.note: Phonology chapter is Alamblak only. In the Sepik Hill comparative chapter Watakataui ('Wat.') appears only in lexicostatistic and sound-correspondence tables (data from Dye & Townsend wordlists). Footnote 1 on p. 514: 'Lewis and Lewis (1970) indicate that stress occurs on the first syllable of the word in Sanio-Hiowe. Stress typically occurs on the penultima in Sumariup and Alamblak.. Dye and Dye (1969) give evidence for phonemic tone-stress in Bahinemo' — Watakataui is not mentioned anywhere regarding stress.

sources.citation: Bruce, Leslie P. Jr. 1975. Alamblak alveopalatals — dead portmanteaus. In R. Conrad, W. Dye, N. Thomson & L. P. Bruce (eds), Papers in New Guinea Linguistics No. 18, 91-106. Pacific Linguistics A-40.
sources.note: Watakataui appears only in Table 1 (p. 100), a Sepik Hill alveopalatal vs alveolar correspondence table. The one stress remark (p. 101, 'Non-phonemic stress [ˈ] is indicated immediately preceding the stressed syllable') concerns the Alamblak transcription. Nothing on Watakataui stress.
